Text.Text: 'And when I fail, I answer for it.' You never had to speak that line, and I am glad beyond the telling. The wards are whole, the halls keep their watch, and the oath has a living answer again. Wherever you stand now, the people beside you are safer than they know. That is the whole of the discipline. Go gently, Guardian.

'While I stand, none fall.' That is the first line of the guardian's oath, and I will not speak the rest to you yet. These halls test only blades with nothing left to learn of themselves. Master the lightsaber wholly, every form the enclave keeps, and return to hear the second line.

'While I stand, none fall.' Do you know the line that follows? Few do, anymore. I am Miris Aven, sentinel of the Jedi Enclave Trial Halls here on Dantooine, and the students who should have learned that second line have barred the training wards and turned their guard inward. Six adepts of the guardian discipline hold the outer ward, protecting no one but themselves. End their watch and recover the Guardian Master Enclave Trial Slate they swore upon. An abandoned oath should not remain in the keeping of those who abandoned it.

So sworn, then, and I will hold you to it as gently as I am able. Take the key, keep to the lamplit colonnade, and do not linger where the light has died. Six adepts. One slate. And come back whole. That is the part of every promise people forget to keep.

A promise weighed line by line. While I stand, none fall. Not for my own hand do I draw. The discipline you seek was never about the blade. It is placement, patience, and the willingness to take a blow meant for someone smaller. The adepts within learned the strength and unlearned the promise, and that is the most dangerous student there is.

The trial halls stand east of the enclave courts, here on Dantooine, behind doors I sealed with my own hands when the students turned. The key I will place in yours unbars them. Past the threshold, follow the colonnade until the lamplight stops. The outer ward is the first hall in darkness. They snuffed the lamps themselves. Guardians, hiding from their own watchman. It grieves me to say it plainly.

Worry is fitting. Fear is optional. They fight as guardians are taught, shield-first, patient, punishing every rash step. But they guard only each other now, and that is weakness dressed as devotion. Do not let them draw you into the dark between the lamps, and do not hate them. Pity keeps a better edge.
The outer ward is still dark, and the Enclave Trial Slate still lies with the adepts who forsook it. A promise delayed is not yet a promise broken. See that it stays so.
You carry something with the weight of an old promise about it. Show me the slate.

So it is. Every guardian of this enclave swore their first line upon this slate. I did, at fifteen, with my hand shaking. I will see it cleaned and returned to its alcove. You have relit the outer ward in the way that matters. Rest now. The second line is heavier, and you have earned the hearing of it.

'Not for my own hand do I draw.' The second line, and the first one the specialists broke. Five of them hold the middle ward, veterans who taught the adepts everything but the promise. They have taken the Guardian Master Kyber Focus Shard from the meditation shrine and set it burning at the heart of their vigil, a guardian's focus bent to guard nothing but their own strength. Defeat the five and carry the shard back to me. It has heard too many wrong prayers already.

You shame students who studied here ten years, speaking so. Go, then. The middle ward lies past the second seal, and your key answers it. Let their wall turn to face you, wait for it, and when you lift the shard, lift it gently. It has been afraid for some time. Yes. Kyber can be afraid.

Themselves. Their pride. The memory of being needed. A guardian without a charge will invent one, and they have invented a fortress where a school should stand. Five shields locked in a ring, facing out at a world that asked nothing of them but their word.

Kyber remembers what is asked of it. That shard sat in the shrine for three generations, and every guardian who knelt before a trial asked it the same thing: let me be enough. It hums with all those askings. In the specialists' keeping it is learning a new question, let them be less, and kyber learns what it is taught. Bring it home before the lesson takes.

As one wall. They will let you spend yourself against them and answer only when you tire, so do not oblige them. Strike, withdraw, make the wall keep choosing a front. A ring of shields defends poorly when it cannot decide where you are. And respect their patience. It is the true veteran in that room.
Five shields still ring the shrine-fire in the middle ward, and the Kyber Focus Shard still hums their wrong question back to them. Every day it burns there, it learns them a little better.
I hear it from here. The shard, singing an old song again. Show me.

Let me hold it. ... There. It remembers the shrine. Whatever they taught it, you have begun the unteaching simply by carrying it kindly. The middle ward stands empty, and the second line stands kept. Two lines remain, and beyond them the ward that broke my heart. Sleep first. That is the oath's own arithmetic, not mere kindness.

'Between harm and the helpless, my blade.' The third line. The warden of these halls spoke it at her investiture with a voice that stilled the pillars. She holds the third ward now against all comers, wearing the Guardian Master Fractured Trial Sigil, the seal of her office, split down its face the day she turned it against the enclave. I ask the hardest thing yet: end her watch and bring the sigil home. And hear the ward-law that binds this trial. A guardian is never tested alone, for the oath requires someone to guard. Take two companions past that seal, or it will not open for you at all.

It is unbarred to the three of you, and to no fewer. The ward itself will know the count. When her guard opens, it opens for a single breath; one of you will see it, so trust whichever of you does. And if she speaks of the students she lost, listen. It will not stay your blade, but it should slow your judgment.

Because the trial is the oath in miniature. A guardian alone is merely a duelist; the discipline lives in the space between you and the one you keep standing. And because the warden has outlasted every blade that came to her alone. Not through cruelty. Through a defense that simply does not end. Bring two you would take a blow for. She will test exactly that, and nothing less will open her guard.

The warden's sigil witnesses every trial held in these halls; no rite above the third ward stands without it. It fractured in the hour she sealed that ward, for such seals answer to the oath and not to the officer. She wears the halves fitted together, as though a broken witness could still testify. Recovering it is not trophy-taking. It is returning the court to the law.

Grief, I believe, though she would name it clarity. She kept the third ward through the raid years and lost students she had sworn over. Somewhere in that loss she decided the only charge worth guarding is the guard itself. It is the oath folded inward until it faces nothing. I prayed for a long time that words could answer her. I have stopped.

The third ward remains sealed to any who come alone; that law is older than either of us. The warden waits within, and the Fractured Trial Sigil with her. Two companions, no fewer, and patience for a defense that does not end. It does end. Barely, and only for a breath.
The pillars are still. They have not been still since her investiture. Tell me it is finished, and show me the sigil.

Both halves, still fitted together. She kept them joined to the last, and that tells me something of her I intend to keep. You stood between harm and each other, and the ward-law counts that as the third line spoken true. I will sit with this awhile after you go. Forgive me. Even a sentinel is allowed one hour of grief.

'Until the last is safe, I hold.' The fourth line belonged to the four ward-captains, the inner circle who stood at the corners of every high trial. They hold the deep ward now, a square with no one inside it to protect, and they keep the Guardian Master Council Trial Chit, the council's token naming a discipline fit to be taught. While they hold it, their inward oath is the official one. Defeat the four and return the chit to the council's keeping. Bring help if it can be had. A square of guardians has no unguarded side.

Then the deep ward is yours to enter; your key answers its seal now, I have seen to it. Remember: the corners, never the center. There is nothing at their center, and that absence is the whole sorrow of them. Go carefully. The fourth line is very nearly the whole oath.

A small thing. Bronzium, plain as a door key, with the whole authority of the enclave council pressed into it. It certifies that what these halls teach is the guardian's discipline and not a private doctrine. Their claim to it is the difference between four traitors and, in their own telling, four custodians. Take it back, and their telling ends.

Corners. Each guards the next, so every strike you land is answered from your blind side. Break the square and they are only four strong blades; leave it whole and they are one creature with eight arms. If companions stand with you, set them to pull two corners apart. The square cannot mourn its shape and fight you at once.

They stood my own investiture, all four. When I spoke the fifth line, it was their blades arched above me. I tell you this not to soften your hand but to steady mine, and because you should know what it is you end. Not villains. Guardians who forgot that holding means holding for someone. Write that on the deep ward wall when it is done, if you have the heart.
The square still stands in the deep ward, four corners about an empty center, with the Council Trial Chit inside it. Corners first. The center will fall on its own. It was never holding anything.
Four ward-captains, and the deep ward open at your back. I have dreaded this hour for a year, and you carry it in like the day's post. The chit, please.

The council convenes tomorrow and will find its token waiting for them, which will discomfort them wonderfully. Four lines of the oath now stand kept. Only the fifth remains, behind the last seal, with the one who taught me every line I know. I must tell you of the Paragon before you face it. But not tonight. Tonight, be somewhere warm.

'And when I fail, I answer for it.' The fifth line, and I have never had to speak it in earnest. Behind the last seal waits the one who taught it to me: the Guardian Master Paragon, first blade of these halls. Understand what stands there. The guard that does not break, the ward that holds until the last is safe, every discipline you have bled for, the Paragon is all of it perfected and turned to the keeping of an empty hall. There is no relic to bring me this time. The Paragon's defeat is itself the testimony. And the ward-law holds at the last seal as it held at the third: no one faces the Paragon alone. The oath requires someone to guard. Bring two, and let the Paragon see you guarding them. It is the only argument that blade has ever respected.

That is the fifth line beginning, whether you hear it yet or not. The last seal has known your key since the deep ward fell. Walk slowly on the way in. Not for tactics. Because you will want to remember these halls as they were, before they become yours to keep.

The finest keeper of the oath these halls ever raised. Every line kept, every charge brought home, every ward held through years that broke lesser sentinels. Every oath but one. When the students turned inward, the Paragon was sworn to answer for the failure, and instead sealed the doors and mounted guard over the failure itself. A perfect watch, kept over nothing at all. That is the one broken line, and it has been breaking further every year since.

You do not. You fight the choice inside it. The Paragon's guard covers one charge without flaw, but you will be three, and a guardian cannot unsee an unguarded friend. Each time that blade turns to answer a threat against one of you, the guard must choose, and in the choosing there is a seam. Be the threat. Then be the charge. Trade the two roles faster than the guard can settle, and hold your nerve when it feels like the ward is holding you. It will feel exactly so.

They open. Students return, the lamps are lit, and the trials resume under the council's seal as they ran for three hundred years. And the discipline of the Guardian Master passes to you. Not a title. A weight. I will not pretend it is light. I will promise you it is the good kind, and that you have carried four lines of it already and stood straighter under each.

The last seal stands open, and the Guardian Master Paragon keeps a perfect watch beyond it. Three of you, no fewer, and remember what I said of the seam: it lives in the choosing. The oath is nearly home.
The lamps in the last hall are burning. I did not light them. Tell me what happened, and leave nothing out. I will keep every word.

Then it is spoken and kept, every line, by you. The Paragon kept every oath but one, and you have answered for that one. The halls open at dawn, the council will set your name in the trial rolls, and the discipline of the Guardian Master is yours to carry and to teach. One thing more, and then rest. When you swear a student of your own someday, and you will, tell them the oath was never five lines. It is one line said five ways: stand where you are needed. Go well, Guardian.
Tell me the charge once more.
Then I'll go and end their watch. The slate comes back with me.
What is the guardian's oath?
How do I reach the outer ward?
Six adepts. Should I be worried?
I can't swear to it today.
The Enclave Trial Slate. Their watch is ended.
Go back. I have another question.
I'll draw for the shrine, not for myself. The shard comes home.
What do the specialists guard in there?
What is the focus shard to your order?
How do five veteran shields fight?
Not yet. That line is heavier than the first.
It sang the whole way here. Take it.
Let me ask something else.
I'll bring two I'd take a blow for. Unbar the seal.
Why must I bring two others?
What is the sigil she carries?
What turned the warden?
Not until two I trust can stand with me.
The third ward is open. Here is her sigil.
Back to the deep ward. Ask me again.
I'll break the square and bring the council its chit.
What is the council chit?
How do the four of them fight?
Were they yours, once?
Not yet. A square with no unguarded side wants more than I have today.
The square is broken. Here is the council's chit.
Speak the whole charge again.
We go together, all three. Let the Paragon watch me guard them.
Who is the Paragon?
How do I fight a perfect guard?
What happens to the halls when it's done?
Not yet. If the Paragon is to see me guarding someone, it must be the right someone.
The Paragon's watch is ended. We guarded each other, and the guard chose wrong.
